一个订阅通过一个消费者读取它的全部主题和分区；workers(n, by_key) 把消息分到按分区键划分的工作分区上。
PulsarBroker::new 只记录配置，connect 构建客户端，启动时为每个订阅打开一个消费者，关闭时关闭生产者。
一条 Pulsar 消息在 RustStream 服务中的路径：消费者、驱动任务、处理器、应答和确认。
Pulsar 主题位于某个租户的命名空间中；持久化主题把消息保存在 BookKeeper 中，分区主题就是每个分区一个主题。
Pulsar 消费者确认一条消息，或者请求再次投递它；客户端在超时后也会请求，并把回来次数过多的消息移到一边。
pulsar 客户端通过服务 URL 查找每个主题，每个 Broker 保持一个连接，并在流量许可范围内向每个消费者推送消息。
Pulsar 订阅是 Broker 保存的一个具名游标；每个订阅都接收整个主题，订阅类型决定它的消费者如何共享它。
ack、drop、retry 和 retry_after 在 Pulsar 上变成什么：确认，以及 Broker 计入客户端死信策略的重新投递。
The parts of ruststream-pulsar a Pulsar service uses, one page per component.
With asyncapi the document speaks Pulsar: each topic's namespace and persistence, and each consumer under x-ruststream-pulsar.
A topic's channel carries the pulsar binding: its namespace and persistence, for subscriptions and publish destinations alike.
A receive operation reports its consumer under x-ruststream-pulsar: the subscription, its type, the ack timeout, topics or pattern.
The server reports the host and port of the service URL, never a token or credentials, and no protocol version.
PulsarBroker connects a service to Pulsar; new only records the service URL, and the runtime dials it once at startup.
PulsarError is the crate's one error type: connect, subscribe, receive, publish, an invalid descriptor and a closed connection.
max_message_size is the largest payload a publish may carry, five mebibytes as on the server; a larger one fails before it is sent.
OperationRetries bounds how long the client keeps retrying an operation a server has not accepted, which is unbounded by default.
One glob, ruststream_pulsar::prelude, brings the core prelude, the broker, its descriptor, positions, context keys and Publish.
token attaches a JWT to the connection, pulsar+ssl:// dials the TLS listener, and credentials never reach the generated document.
Shutdown closes the producers the crate opened, and a publisher or a seek used afterwards reports PulsarError::NotConnected.
At startup the runtime dials the service URL, then opens a consumer per subscription; a refused descriptor stops the start.
PulsarContext gives a handler where its delivery sits in the log and the handle that moves the subscription, each read through Ctx.
A batch handler's context carries the subscription's seek handle alone; asking a batch for Position does not compile.
PulsarPosition names a place in a topic's retained log: either end, a delivered message, or a publish time.
A handler moves its whole subscription through the SeekHandle key; queued deliveries are dropped and replay starts at the target.
start_at seeks a subscription to a position on every startup, rewinding its durable cursor, unlike Pulsar's initial position.
PulsarPublish, Publish in the prelude, opens one producer per topic and waits for the broker's receipt, so Ok means stored.
A header travels as a Pulsar message property, one per header and no envelope; a value that is not UTF-8 fails the publish.
The partition-key header is the message key: it picks the partition of a partitioned topic and orders KeyShared and by_key lanes.
The partition_key step keys one publish from a handler body; it wins over a partition-key header and keeps the slot's codec.
ack acknowledges a Pulsar delivery, retry negatively acknowledges it, and drop acknowledges it too: Pulsar has no terminal reject.
ack_timeout redelivers a message left unacknowledged longer than the timeout; it also bounds the delay a retry_after may ask for.
max_attempts with dead_letter becomes the consumer's own dead-letter policy: the client moves a spent message, and the service publishes nothing.
retry_after holds the delivery unacknowledged in the service for the delay, then negatively acknowledges it; nothing is republished.
A topic in #[subscriber] joins the broker's default subscription on it; a PulsarSubscription carries every other setting.
A slice handler takes a batch the service assembles: full at the mount site's size, or closed batch_wait after its first delivery.
PulsarSubscription::pattern reads every topic whose full name matches a regular expression, topics created later included.
PulsarSubscription::new joins a named durable subscription on one topic: a bare name, tenant/namespace/topic, or a full name.
PulsarTopic is a topic name checked on construction: persistent and non_persistent for literals, parse for names read at run time.
SubscriptionType says how the consumers of one subscription share it: Exclusive, Shared, Failover or KeyShared.
PulsarSubscription::topics reads a fixed list of topics under one subscription; one seek or one retry policy covers them all.
TestApp::start connects PulsarBroker in process: topics, the four subscription types, dead letters, delayed retries and seeking.
TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running Pulsar, for what only a server has.

ruststream-pulsar 如何测量自己：三个循环、在真实 Broker 上的运行、受 Broker 限制的判定计算，以及代码计数。流程就是框架自己的流程（RustStream 方法论），本页说明它在 Pulsar 上是什么样子。

一个进程把每个场景跑三遍，作为三个循环，它们只有一处不同：承载消息的是什么。 裸客户端。 一个 pulsar crate 的消费者，直接驱动：接收、解码、确认。 Broker crate。 本 crate，上面什么也没有：Broker 建立连接，PulsarSubscription 打开订阅，一个循环从它的流中取出投递、解码并 ack。 RustStream。 用户写的服务：一个 #[subscriber] 处理器及其外围的应用。 其余一切在三个循环中都相同：订阅及其类型、ack 的位置、解码成同一个结构体、载荷字节、带四个工作线程的 tokio 运行时，以及二进制程序。 消息体是 128 字节的 JSON。它解码成一个包含两个整数字段的结构体，因此解码不做内存分配，数字反映的是本 crate，而不是 JSON 解析器。

每次运行使用新的主题和新的订阅。 主题是持久化的、不分区的，位于 public/default 命名空间中，运行结束后通过管理 API 删除，因此一次运行永远看不到之前的运行留下的东西。 消费者先接入。 然后由第二个连接上的生产者向它发送消息，最多领先消费者已处理的消息 20 000 条。 在三个循环中，计时窗口都从第一次投递开始，到最后一次确认结束。 建立连接、订阅和创建主题都在窗口之外。确认是写入套接字的一条命令，不等待应答，因此任何循环都看不到服务器记录它。 消息条数来自一次探测，它在 50 000 条消息上测量裸循环的速率，因此在任何机器上，测量的运行都至少持续五秒。 各循环交替进行：裸、crate、RustStream，共三轮。每个循环报告它最佳、中位和最差的一轮。 当裸客户端在运行中一直在等传输时，该行标为 受 Broker 限制。这是算出来的：在各轮之外，一次探测为一次主题查找及其应答计时，这是客户端要等待的最便宜的请求。消费者本身不等待任何往返：它预先授予接收许可，确认也不等应答。但每次投递背后确实有一次往返，即它之前的那次发布，生产者会一直等到 Broker 存储了消息。这次往返达到每条消息测得时间的一半时，该行就被标记。往返时间与机器信息一起公布，因此这个计算可以核对。

开销图的每个场景都是用户写的服务，基于 PulsarBroker，连接同一个 Broker，构建时不带 testing 特性。一个 Shared 订阅读取本次运行专用的持久化主题。另一个线程用自己的运行时和连接，在测量区间打开之前通过本 crate 的发布者填充主题，因此在服务取走第一条消息之前，每条消息都已存储。 指令数来自 callgrind，内存分配来自 DHAT。一个场景依次在一次投递、1000 次、2000 次上运行。后两次之差是一条消息的稳态开销，单次投递就是冷启动。 与保存的基线对照时，任何场景的指令数多出百分之二就算失败。内存分配在每次运行中都受每个场景声明的下限约束。

just bench 这条命令按 docker-compose.test.yml 启动测试环境，运行两个对照场景，停止测试环境，并重写 docs/benchmarks/results.json。它需要几分钟，并且需要独占机器。它会清空 RUSTFLAGS，因此二进制程序不会绑定到构建它的 CPU 上。两条命令都按发布版本的方式构建基准测试，跨 crate 启用完整的链接时优化（fat LTO），因此这些数字描述的正是服务实际使用的代码。 just bench-code 代码计数需要一两分钟，并且需要 valgrind。just bench-code 5000 在更大的条数上测量，得到更稳定的数字。在 main 上运行 just bench-code --save-baseline=main 记录基线，在分支上运行 just bench-code --baseline=main 与它对照。
ruststream-pulsar 的基准测试数字测的是什么，以及不能从中得出哪些结论。

同一行中的三个循环可以互相比较，因为它们在同一个进程中、交替地、对着同一个 Broker 运行。一行不能与另一个 Broker crate 公布的行比较：各种传输在每条消息上做的工作不同。 Broker 运行在同一台机器上，走回环接口。没有网络延迟，同样的每条消息开销在时间中所占的比例，比面对跨网络的集群时更大。应把该百分比读作已部署服务所付代价的上界。 受 Broker 限制 的行表示每次投递背后的发布回执已经占去一次投递所用时间的一半。本 crate 和运行时的工作于是发生在这段等待之内，测出的差异接近零。这是开销的下界，而不是对它的测量。
指令计数包含本 crate 的代码、它上面的运行时，以及 pulsar 客户端在服务线程上的工作。每个数字的大部分属于客户端。由于 Broker 是真实的，计数在各次运行之间会有少许变动。同样的计数在缓存未命中处要花更多时间，因此计数不等于时间。 每个数字都是稳态，即 1000 次投递的运行与 2000 次投递的运行之差。建立连接、订阅以及它们背后的首批内存分配属于冷启动，只付一次。

一行就是一个消费者读取默认命名空间中一个持久化、不分区的主题，消息体很小，Pulsar 以单机模式运行在一个容器中。它测量的是一次投递在本 crate 内部的开销，而不是 Pulsar 能承载多少。 分区主题、一个订阅的多个消费者和一组工作分区各自回答不同的问题，这个对照不测量其中任何一个。代码图在同一测试环境上统计批处理器和应答。 这些数字是一台机器在某一天的快照，构建信息记录在旁边。它们在一台只做这次运行的机器上手动重新测量：它们显示的差异小于共享机器的噪声。

The parts of ruststream-pulsar a Pulsar service uses, one page per component, grouped by the part of the service they belong to. The broker, PulsarBroker, holds the connection. A subscription names its topics with a descriptor, and a handler's outcome becomes an acknowledgement. A handler reads where its delivery sits through its context, and moves its subscription to a position in the log. A service publishes through a policy, with a key and headers per message. The Pulsar bindings describe the service in its AsyncAPI document, and a TestApp test runs it on an in-process transport.

With the asyncapi feature the generated document speaks Pulsar: each topic's namespace and persistence, and each consumer under x-ruststream-pulsar. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. This crate adds what it knows about the Pulsar side. A server reports the host and the port of the service URL. A channel carries the specification's pulsar binding, version 0.1.0: the namespace and the persistence of the topic behind it. The specification's Pulsar operation binding has no fields, so a receive operation reports its consumer under the extension key x-ruststream-pulsar. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker, the descriptors and the destinations the mount sites resolved. A subscription by bare topic name carries no descriptor, so its channel and its operation carry no binding. The document is published and shared, so no binding carries a token or a credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-pulsar = { version = "0.8", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label pulsar, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example pulsar_asyncapi --features asyncapi -- asyncapi gen prints the document. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "1.0.0")).with_broker_labeled("pulsar", broker, |b| { b.include(confirm).include(regional).include(audit) }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let token = env::var("PULSAR_TOKEN").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&token)) } examples/manual/pulsar_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "1.0.0")).with_broker_labeled("pulsar", broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("persistent://acme/orders/created", "confirmations") .ack_timeout(Duration::from_secs(30)), Confirm, ) .reply() .to("persistent://acme/orders/confirmed") .build(), ) .include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::topics( ["persistent://acme/eu/orders", "persistent://acme/us/orders"], "regional", ) .subscription_type(SubscriptionType::KeyShared), Regional, ) .build(), ) .include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::pattern("audit-.*", "auditors"), Audit).build()) }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let token = env::var("PULSAR_TOKEN").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&token)) }

A topic's channel carries the pulsar binding: its namespace and persistence, for subscriptions and publish destinations alike. The binding has two fields, read off the topic name. persistent://acme/orders/created has the namespace orders and the persistence persistent; a non-persistent:// topic reports non-persistent. A PulsarSubscription::new reads one topic and reports it. A topics subscription reports the binding when all its topics share one namespace and one persistence. Its channel is named after the subscription. A pattern subscription has no topic until it lists the server's topics, so its channel carries no binding. A channel the service publishes to reports the topic the mount site resolved. That is a reply("dest") clause, a reply type's #[outgoing(name)], the name of a slot entry, or a declared dead-letter topic. A destination that is not a valid topic name carries no binding.

The channel persistent://acme/orders/created reports the namespace orders, and so does the reply destination persistent://acme/orders/confirmed. The channel regional spans two namespaces and the pattern channel auditors names no topic, so neither carries a binding. The extension carries what a reader of the document most wants to know about a consumer: Field Value subscription the durable subscription the consumer joins subscriptionType Exclusive, Shared, Failover or KeyShared ackTimeoutMillis the ack timeout, when the descriptor sets one topics every topic of a topics subscription topicPattern the regular expression of a pattern subscription The values come from the descriptor alone, before the broker connects. A subscription by bare topic name has no descriptor, so its operation carries no extension.

The operation receive_persistent___acme_orders_created reports the subscription confirmations, of the default type Shared, with a 30-second ack timeout. The server reports the host and port of the service URL, never a token or credentials, and no protocol version. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its host is the host and the port of the service URL: the pulsar:// or pulsar+ssl:// scheme and any user info stay out of it. The protocol is pulsar for both schemes. protocolVersion stays out, because a Pulsar client and the server agree on the protocol version per connection. The token the broker authenticates with is not part of the server. A test that builds the document with a token in the broker finds the token nowhere in it.

The broker dials the TLS listener of pulsar.acme.internal and authenticates with a token. Its server in the document is pulsar.acme.internal:6651 with the protocol pulsar. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_asyncapi.rs /// The cluster's TLS listener, authenticated with a JWT. fn broker(token: &str) -> PulsarBroker { PulsarBroker::new("pulsar+ssl://pulsar.acme.internal:6651").token(token) } examples/manual/pulsar_asyncapi.rs /// The cluster's TLS listener, authenticated with a JWT. fn broker(token: &str) -> PulsarBroker { PulsarBroker::new("pulsar+ssl://pulsar.acme.internal:6651").token(token) }

PulsarBroker connects a service to Pulsar; new only records the service URL, and the runtime dials it once at startup. PulsarBroker::new takes one service URL, pulsar://host:6650 or pulsar+ssl://host:6651. It does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. The settings that follow it are builder steps too: the token, the default subscription of a bare topic name, the operation retries and the payload limit. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedPulsarBroker. Every subscription and every publisher of the service opens over that one connection. At shutdown the runtime closes the producers the handlers published through. A subscription names its topic and its durable subscription in a PulsarSubscription. #[subscriber("orders")] names the topic alone and joins the broker's default subscription on it, as the Subscriptions page shows. Building the crate needs protoc on the path, because the client compiles the Pulsar protocol definitions. Two features add to the crate: testing connects the broker in process for TestApp, and asyncapi fills in the Pulsar part of the generated document. Getting started runs a first service against a local Pulsar.

The service reads the topic orders in the shared subscription workers. An order with no items comes back, at most five deliveries in all, and then moves to the topic orders-dlq. cargo run --example pulsar_service --features testing -- run starts it against a Pulsar on localhost:6650. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_service.rs use std::time::Duration; use ruststream_pulsar::prelude::*; #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "workers") .subscription_type(SubscriptionType::Shared) .ack_timeout(Duration::from_secs(30)) )] async fn handle(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.items == 0 { // Comes back, up to five deliveries in all, then moves to `orders-dlq`. tracing::warn!(subscription = "workers", order.id, "order has no items yet"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.items, "order received"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/pulsar_service.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(handle) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5)) .dead_letter("orders-dlq") }, ) } examples/manual/pulsar_service.rs use std::time::Duration; use ruststream_pulsar::prelude::*; struct HandleOrder; impl Handle<Order> for HandleOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.items == 0 { // Comes back, up to five deliveries in all, then moves to `orders-dlq`. tracing::warn!(subscription = "workers", order.id, "order has no items yet"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.items, "order received"); ready(Ok(())) } } examples/manual/pulsar_service.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { // The shared subscription `workers` on `orders`. b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "workers") .subscription_type(SubscriptionType::Shared) .ack_timeout(Duration::from_secs(30)), HandleOrder, ) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5)) .dead_letter("orders-dlq") }, ) }

PulsarError is the crate's one error type: connect, subscribe, receive, publish, an invalid descriptor and a closed connection. Each variant names the step that failed. The client's error behind it is its source, so the client library's types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect the client could not parse the service URL or connect with it Subscribe the server refused a consumer, naming the topic or the pattern Receive an open consumer's stream failed or ended Publish a producer could not open, the server refused a message, the payload is over max_message_size, or a header value is not UTF-8 text NotConnected a publisher or a seek was used after the broker shut down Invalid a descriptor or a destination is not valid: an empty name, a malformed topic, a pattern that is no regular expression, a bare name with no default subscription A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

A shipment the broker refuses is logged with its cause, and the order is settled as a retry. After three deliveries the order moves to its dead-letter topic. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_errors.rs #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "shipping"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher, Shipments>) -> HandlerOutcome { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, labels: (1..=order.parcels) .map(|parcel| format!("{}-{parcel:06}", order.id)) .collect(), }; if let Err(err) = shipments.message(&shipment).publish().await { // The error names the topic and the reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "shipping", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not published"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_errors.rs struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, labels: (1..=order.parcels) .map(|parcel| format!("{}-{parcel:06}", order.id)) .collect(), }; if let Err(err) = outs.get(Shipments).message(&shipment).publish().await { // The error names the topic and the reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "shipping", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not published"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } }

max_message_size is the largest payload a publish may carry, five mebibytes as on the server; a larger one fails before it is sent. The default matches the server's own maxMessageSize. A deployment that changed that setting sets the same number here, in bytes. A publish over the limit returns PulsarError::Publish, naming the topic, and nothing leaves the service. The check matters because a server answers an oversized frame by dropping the connection, and every producer and consumer on that connection fails with it. A handler that receives the error decides how its delivery settles. Retrying cannot make a payload smaller, so a handler usually logs it and drops the delivery or settles it some other final way. A TestApp test refuses the same publishes in process. Connecting to a production cluster sets the message size a cluster accepts.

The cluster runs with a one-mebibyte limit. A scan that encodes to more is logged and dropped; a smaller one is archived. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_limits.rs #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("uploads", "archiver"))] async fn archive(upload: &Upload, Out(scans): Out<impl Publisher, Archive>) -> HandlerOutcome { let scan = Scan { upload_id: upload.id, pages: (1..=upload.pages) .map(|page| format!("page-{page:06}")) .collect(), }; if let Err(err) = scans.message(&scan).publish().await { // Retrying cannot shrink the scan, so it is logged and dropped. tracing::warn!(subscription = "archiver", upload.id, error = %err, "scan not archived"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The cluster runs with `maxMessageSize=1048576`. let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").max_message_size(nonzero!(1_048_576usize)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("archive", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(archive).out(Archive, Publish)) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_limits.rs struct ArchiveUpload; impl<Entry> Handle<Upload, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for ArchiveUpload where Entry: OutEntry<Archive, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, upload: &Upload, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let scan = Scan { upload_id: upload.id, pages: (1..=upload.pages) .map(|page| format!("page-{page:06}")) .collect(), }; if let Err(err) = outs.get(Archive).message(&scan).publish().await { // Retrying cannot shrink the scan, so it is logged and dropped. tracing::warn!(subscription = "archiver", upload.id, error = %err, "scan not archived"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The cluster runs with `maxMessageSize=1048576`. let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").max_message_size(nonzero!(1_048_576usize)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("archive", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("uploads", "archiver"), ArchiveUpload, ) .build(), ) .out(Archive, Publish) }) }

OperationRetries bounds how long the client keeps retrying an operation a server has not accepted, which is unbounded by default. A server sometimes answers "not now": a broker is still starting, a topic is moving between brokers, a subscription is taken. The client then tries again, by default for ever and five seconds apart. That is what waits out a broker restart. attempts(n) gives up after n tries and reports what the server answered. One try makes the first answer final. delay sets the wait between tries, five seconds by default, and timeout the time one try has to be answered, thirty seconds by default. PulsarBroker::operation_retries applies the bound. The bound covers every retried operation of the connection: topic lookups, opening producers and consumers, and a consumer's reconnect after a disconnect. A short bound turns a long outage into a subscription that gives up. The case that needs a bound is an Exclusive subscription another consumer holds. Unbounded, the second consumer waits for the first to leave, and the service does not start. Bounded, startup fails with PulsarError::Subscribe, naming the topic. In a TestApp test the in-process transport refuses a second Exclusive consumer at once, so the bound shows only against a server. Connecting to a production cluster bounds the retries of a service and tests the configuration.

The ledger has one writer at a time. A second instance of the service tries three times, a second apart, and then fails its startup instead of waiting. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_retries.rs /// The cluster at `url`; an operation the server keeps refusing fails after three tries. fn broker(url: &str) -> PulsarBroker { PulsarBroker::new(url) .operation_retries(OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(3u32)).delay(Duration::from_secs(1))) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("pulsar://localhost:6650")) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_retries.rs /// The cluster at `url`; an operation the server keeps refusing fails after three tries. fn broker(url: &str) -> PulsarBroker { PulsarBroker::new(url) .operation_retries(OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(3u32)).delay(Duration::from_secs(1))) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("pulsar://localhost:6650"), ledger("ledger")) }

One glob, ruststream_pulsar::prelude, brings the core prelude, the broker, its descriptor, positions, context keys and Publish. use ruststream_pulsar::prelude::*; is the one import a Pulsar routes file writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds PulsarBroker and OperationRetries, the descriptor PulsarSubscription with SubscriptionType and PulsarTopic, the positions PulsarPosition and PulsarSeeker, and the context types with their keys Position and SeekHandle. The core traits Positioned and Seeker come with them. The publish policy comes under the name every broker crate uses: Publish is PulsarPublish. So a mount site reads the same on every broker. Two broker preludes in one file collide on this name; the prefixed type at the crate root tells them apart. A handler body bounds its slots with capability traits, such as Out<impl Publisher>, and names no broker type. The one exception is a body that keys a publish: partition_key needs PulsarPublishSteps in scope and the slot bounded Out<impl Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions>, Marker>, both from this prelude.

The descriptor, its subscription type, the broker's retries and the reply policy all come from the one glob. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_pulsar::prelude::*; #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "confirmations-svc") .subscription_type(SubscriptionType::KeyShared), reply )] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650") .operation_retries(OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(5u32))); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish)) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_pulsar::prelude::*; struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650") .operation_retries(OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(5u32))); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "confirmations-svc") .subscription_type(SubscriptionType::KeyShared), Confirm, ) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) }) }

token attaches a JWT to the connection, pulsar+ssl:// dials the TLS listener, and credentials never reach the generated document. token is Pulsar's token authentication: the client sends the JWT when it connects and when it reconnects. A service reads the token from its environment or its secret store, as the example does. A pulsar+ssl:// URL dials the server's TLS listener, port 6651 by convention. The client verifies the server's certificate against the system's trusted roots and checks its host name. The connection is TLS from the first byte, so the URL is the whole setting. A TestApp test runs the same broker in process. It checks the URL as the client parses it, and the token goes nowhere. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the host and the port, and never the token or a user name in the URL. Connecting to a production cluster takes the service URL and the token from the environment.

The service authenticates with the token in PULSAR_TOKEN and talks to the cluster over TLS. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_security.rs /// The cluster's TLS listener, authenticated with a JWT. fn broker(token: &str) -> PulsarBroker { PulsarBroker::new("pulsar+ssl://pulsar.acme.internal:6651").token(token) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let token = env::var("PULSAR_TOKEN").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&token)) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_security.rs /// The cluster's TLS listener, authenticated with a JWT. fn broker(token: &str) -> PulsarBroker { PulsarBroker::new("pulsar+ssl://pulsar.acme.internal:6651").token(token) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let token = env::var("PULSAR_TOKEN").unwrap_or_default(); service(broker(&token)) }

Shutdown closes the producers the crate opened, and a publisher or a seek used afterwards reports PulsarError::NotConnected. The crate opens one producer per topic the service publishes to, on the first publish there. At shutdown it closes each of them, so the server releases them at once. A producer that fails to close is logged and does not fail the shutdown. The client's connection itself ends with the client. The shutdown therefore returns (), with no report of its own. A publisher taken before the shutdown keeps pointing at the closed connection. That includes one taken off the broker before startup with PulsarBroker::publisher. A publish through it returns PulsarError::NotConnected and never succeeds against the dead connection. A seek through a handle that outlived the connection is refused the same way.

The service replies to each order with a shipment, which opens a producer on shipments; shutdown closes it. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_shutdown.rs /// The service on `broker`. Its replies open a producer on `shipments`, which shutdown closes. fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(ship).out_reply(Publish)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650")) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_shutdown.rs /// The service on `broker`. Its replies open a producer on `shipments`, which shutdown closes. fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "shipping"), Ship) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650")) }

At startup the runtime dials the service URL, then opens a consumer per subscription; a refused descriptor stops the start. The connect builds the client and dials the URL once. A URL the client cannot parse fails it with PulsarError::Connect. Each subscription then opens its consumer over that connection. Before any I/O, the crate checks what needs no server and refuses it with PulsarError::Invalid: an empty subscription name or an empty topic list; a topic name Pulsar does not accept; a pattern that is not a regular expression; a retry cap without a dead-letter topic, or the reverse, and a cap on an Exclusive or Failover subscription (see Dead letters); a bare topic name on a broker with no default subscription; the error names that setting. A consumer the server refuses fails with PulsarError::Subscribe, naming the topic. A second consumer of an Exclusive subscription waits for the first to leave, unless OperationRetries bounds the tries. One refused subscription fails the whole startup, and the service exits before it reads anything. A TestApp test refuses the same descriptors, so a service that does not start in production does not start in its tests either.

The service reads orders by its bare name, in the default subscription orders-svc, and every audit-* topic through a pattern. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_broker_startup.rs /// A bare topic name: it joins the broker's default subscription. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// A pattern: checked as a regular expression before its consumer opens. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::pattern("audit-.*", "auditors"))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(place).include(audit)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("orders-svc")) } examples/manual/pulsar_broker_startup.rs struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // A bare topic name: it joins the broker's default subscription. b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()) // A pattern: checked as a regular expression before its consumer opens. .include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::pattern("audit-.*", "auditors"), Audit).build()) }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("orders-svc")) }

PulsarContext gives a handler where its delivery sits in the log and the handle that moves the subscription, each read through Ctx. The subscription builds it once per delivery, beside the payload and the headers, with no allocation. A handler binds one field with Ctx<K>, where K is a key: Key Value What it is Position PulsarPosition the delivery's message id; a seek to it delivers this message again SeekHandle PulsarSeeker the handle that moves the subscription, on every topic it reads Both keys are in the prelude. Ctx<Position> copies the message id, while ctx.context(Position) borrows it. A body that reads both keys takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext> instead and calls ctx.context(key) per key. In the manual form the context is the fourth parameter of Handle: impl Handle<Job, (), (), PulsarContext>. A batch body reads a PulsarBatchContext, which carries the seek handle alone. Replay and seeking reads the seek handle from the context to index every order again.

A job whose result was lost moves the subscription back to its own position, so it is done again. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_context.rs /// Logs where each job sits; a job whose result was lost moves the subscription back to its /// own position, so the job is delivered again. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("jobs", "workers"))] async fn work( job: &Job, ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext>, State(redos): State<Arc<Redos>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, at = ?ctx.context(Position), "job done"); if job.redo && redos.first_time(job) { let at = ctx.context(Position).clone(); if ctx.context(SeekHandle).seek(at).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_context.rs /// Logs where each job sits; a job whose result was lost moves the subscription back to its /// own position, so the job is delivered again. struct Work; impl Handle<Job, (), (), PulsarContext, AppState> for Work { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext, AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { tracing::info!(job.id, at = ?ctx.context(Position), "job done"); if job.redo && ctx.state().redos.first_time(job) { let at = ctx.context(Position).clone(); if ctx.context(SeekHandle).seek(at).await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } Ok(()) } }

A batch handler's context, PulsarBatchContext, carries the subscription's seek handle alone; asking a batch for Position does not compile. A batch spans many deliveries, so it has no single position in the log. The subscription builds the context once per batch, from what every delivery of the batch shares: the SeekHandle key, the same key a PulsarContext carries. A batch body takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarBatchContext> and reads the handle with ctx.context(SeekHandle). A seek from a batch body takes effect once the batch has settled, so the next batch opens at the new position. Position is a compile error in a batch body, because the batch context does not carry it. In the manual form the context is the fourth parameter of Handle: impl Handle<[Job], (), (), PulsarBatchContext>.

A batch that holds a job whose result was lost replays the retained log once. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_context.rs /// A batch with a job whose result was lost settles first; the seek then replays the /// retained log, so the next batch opens at the beginning. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("jobs", "bulk"))] async fn work( jobs: &[Job], ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarBatchContext>, State(redos): State<Arc<Redos>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "jobs done"); let redo = jobs.iter().any(|job| job.redo && redos.first_time(job)); if redo && ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(PulsarPosition::earliest()) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_context.rs /// A batch with a job whose result was lost settles first; the seek then replays the /// retained log, so the next batch opens at the beginning. struct Work; impl Handle<[Job], (), (), PulsarBatchContext, AppState> for Work { async fn handle( &self, jobs: &[Job], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarBatchContext, AppState>, ) -> Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "jobs done"); let redos = &ctx.state().redos; let redo = jobs.iter().any(|job| job.redo && redos.first_time(job)); if redo && ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(PulsarPosition::earliest()) .await .is_err() { return Err(jobs.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()).collect()); } Ok(()) } }

PulsarPosition names a place in a topic's retained log: either end, a delivered message, or a publish time. Pulsar keeps a topic's messages as a log, so a subscription can be moved through it, at startup with start_at or from a handler with a seek. PulsarPosition::earliest() is the oldest message the topic still retains, and every retained message is delivered again from there. PulsarPosition::latest() is the tip of the log: only messages published after the move are delivered. PulsarPosition::timestamp(millis) is the first message published at or after that time, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. A delivery's own place is a position as well: Ctx<Position> binds it through the Position key, a copy the handler can keep. A seek to such a position delivers that message again, then the rest of the log in order. A position applies to every topic and every partition the subscription reads. A non-persistent topic retains nothing, so a move over it replays nothing. Replay and seeking rebuilds balances from a ledger on every startup and indexes every order again with a seek.

A projection bookmarks the entry that closes a day; a rebuild request moves the ledger subscription back to it. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_positions.rs /// Where the projection last closed a day: the ledger subscription's seeker and the position /// of the entry that closed it. #[derive(Clone, Default)] struct Bookmark(Arc<Mutex<Option<(PulsarSeeker, PulsarPosition)>>>); #[derive(FromRef)] struct AppState { bookmark: Bookmark, } /// Projects each ledger entry and bookmarks the entry that closes a day. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("ledger", "projection"))] async fn project( entry: &Entry, Ctx(position): Ctx<Position>, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>, State(bookmark): State<Bookmark>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "projected"); if entry.closes_day { *bookmark.0.lock().await = Some((seeker, position)); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Replays the ledger from the last closed day: the entry at the bookmark comes again, then /// every entry after it, in order. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("ledger.rebuild", "projection"))] async fn rebuild(request: &Rebuild, State(bookmark): State<Bookmark>) -> HandlerOutcome { let Some((seeker, position)) = bookmark.0.lock().await.clone() else { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); }; tracing::info!(reason = %request.reason, "rebuilding from the last closed day"); match seeker.seek(position).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(%err, "the ledger cannot be rewound"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/pulsar_positions.rs /// Where the projection last closed a day: the ledger subscription's seeker and the position /// of the entry that closed it. #[derive(Clone, Default)] struct Bookmark(Arc<Mutex<Option<(PulsarSeeker, PulsarPosition)>>>); struct AppState { bookmark: Bookmark, } /// Projects each ledger entry and bookmarks the entry that closes a day. struct Project; impl Handle<Entry, (), (), PulsarContext, AppState> for Project { async fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext, AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "projected"); if entry.closes_day { let mark = ( ctx.context(SeekHandle).clone(), ctx.context(Position).clone(), ); *ctx.state().bookmark.0.lock().await = Some(mark); } Ok(()) } } /// Replays the ledger from the last closed day: the entry at the bookmark comes again, then /// every entry after it, in order. struct Rewind; impl Handle<Rebuild, (), (), PulsarContext, AppState> for Rewind { async fn handle( &self, request: &Rebuild, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext, AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Some((seeker, position)) = ctx.state().bookmark.0.lock().await.clone() else { return Ok(()); }; tracing::info!(reason = %request.reason, "rebuilding from the last closed day"); seeker.seek(position).await.map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(%err, "the ledger cannot be rewound"); HandlerOutcome::retry() }) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { bookmark: Bookmark::default(), }) }) .with_broker(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("ledger", "projection"), Project).build()) .include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("ledger.rebuild", "projection"), Rewind, ) .build(), ) }) }

A handler moves its whole subscription through the SeekHandle key; queued deliveries are dropped and replay starts at the target. Ctx<SeekHandle> binds a PulsarSeeker for the subscription the delivery came from. Its seek(position) takes a PulsarPosition, and the next delivery comes from there. The seek moves the subscription, not one consumer: every topic and every partition it reads, and every consumer that shares it. Deliveries already queued when the seek lands are dropped, so the handler never sees them. A batch still being assembled is the exception: it closes with the deliveries it had taken. A seeker is a value, so a handler can keep it and move the subscription later from elsewhere, as the PulsarPosition example does. A seek after the service shut down returns PulsarError::NotConnected. A batch handler reaches the same key through its PulsarBatchContext. A position that has to apply on each boot belongs in start_at instead. Replay and seeking indexes every order again with a seek from the handler.

A job marked poisoned starts a run the producer knows to be unprocessable; the subscription jumps to the tip of the log past it. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_positions_seek.rs /// Skips a poisoned run: the subscription jumps to the tip of the log, and the jobs queued /// behind the marker never reach the handler. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("jobs", "workers"))] async fn work(job: &Job, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "worked"); if !job.poisoned { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } match seeker.seek(PulsarPosition::latest()).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(job.id, %err, "the poisoned run cannot be skipped"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/pulsar_positions_seek.rs /// Skips a poisoned run: the subscription jumps to the tip of the log, and the jobs queued /// behind the marker never reach the handler. struct Work; impl Handle<Job, (), (), PulsarContext> for Work { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { tracing::info!(job.id, "worked"); if !job.poisoned { return Ok(()); } ctx.context(SeekHandle) .seek(PulsarPosition::latest()) .await .map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(job.id, %err, "the poisoned run cannot be skipped"); HandlerOutcome::retry() }) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("jobs", "workers"), Work).build()) }) }

start_at seeks a subscription to a position on every startup, rewinding its durable cursor, unlike Pulsar's initial position. It is a clause of the attribute, start_at(PulsarPosition::earliest()), or .start_at(position) among the mount-site settings. A Pulsar subscription is durable state on the broker: its cursor records what was acknowledged, and it outlives the service. The seek lands before the subscription's first delivery, so the handler sees the log from the position on. start_at(PulsarPosition::earliest()) therefore replays the retained backlog each time the service starts, acknowledged messages included. Pulsar's own initial position is different: the broker applies it only when it creates the subscription. A subscription without the clause resumes from its cursor. It suits a read model rebuilt from the retained log on each boot. Replay and seeking rebuilds account balances from a ledger on every startup.

The audit projection is rebuilt from the oldest retained entry on every startup, although its subscription acknowledged everything it read before. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_positions_start_at.rs /// Rebuilds the audit projection from the oldest retained entry on every startup. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("ledger.audit", "audit"), start_at(PulsarPosition::earliest()) )] async fn replay(entry: &AuditEntry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "projected"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_positions_start_at.rs /// Projects every audit entry it reads. struct Replay; impl Handle<AuditEntry> for Replay { fn handle( &self, entry: &AuditEntry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "projected"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The service on the Pulsar cluster `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(PulsarBroker::new(url), |b| { // The projection is rebuilt from the oldest retained entry on every startup. b.include( subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("ledger.audit", "audit"), Replay) .start_at(PulsarPosition::earliest()) .build(), ) }) }

PulsarPublish, Publish in the prelude, opens one producer per topic and waits for the broker's receipt, so Ok means stored. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish) for a slot. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into a PulsarPublisher. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through this one. A reply goes to the topic its type names with #[outgoing(name = "..")], or to the one a reply("..") clause names when the type leaves it open. The publisher opens a producer for a topic on the first publish there and keeps it until shutdown. A publish returns once the broker has stored the message, or with the error it reported. Outside a handler, PulsarBroker::publisher hands out a publisher before the service starts. Per message, a publish carries headers and a key. Publishing and replies confirms orders with receipts and answers price quotes.

A header travels as a Pulsar message property, one per header and no envelope; a value that is not UTF-8 fails the publish. The property has the header's name and value, so a consumer in another language reads it as a plain Pulsar property. The payload stays the encoded message alone. A message type declares its headers in a typed contract, #[outgoing(headers = ..)], and the handler sets them with with_headers. A HeaderMap written by hand works the same. Pulsar properties are text, so a header value that is not valid UTF-8 fails the publish with PulsarError::Publish. On delivery the properties come back as the message's headers. One header has a meaning of its own: the partition-key header becomes the message key. Publishing and replies sends pick lists with headers to warehouses.

The partition-key header, PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, is the message key: it picks the partition of a partitioned topic and orders KeyShared and by_key lanes. The header is named partition-key. On publish its value becomes the Pulsar message key and does not travel as a property of its own. On a partitioned topic the producer hashes the key, so every message of one key goes to one partition, in the order it was published. A publish without a key spreads over the partitions in turn. A message type declares the header in its typed contract, #[outgoing(headers = ..)], with a field renamed to partition-key; a HeaderMap with that entry works the same. On consume the key comes back as that header. A KeyShared subscription hands every message of one key to one consumer, and workers(n, by_key) keeps one key on one lane inside a consumer. A handler body that keys one publish of a slot uses the partition_key step instead. Subscription types and ordering places keyed messages on the partitions of a partitioned topic.

let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; if shipments .message(&shipment) .with_headers(&key) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_publishing_keys.rs /// The header a shipment carries: `partition-key`, which becomes the message key. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct ShipmentKey { #[serde(rename = "partition-key")] customer: String, } /// Every shipment of one customer carries one key, so the partition and the consumer that /// take it see that customer's shipments in order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments", headers = ShipmentKey)] struct Shipment { order_id: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; The partition_key step keys one publish from a handler body; it wins over a partition-key header and keeps the slot's codec. The key does what the partition-key header does: it places the message on a partition and orders KeyShared consumers. The step writes the one field of PulsarPublishOptions and returns the builder. The message still leaves through the slot the mount site wired, in that slot's codec and through its transforms. A body reaches the step by bounding its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions>, Slot>. That body imports ruststream_pulsar::prelude::*, the one case where a handler body names this broker. The mount site declares nothing for it, and a publish without the step goes unkeyed. Where a publish carries both the step and the header, the step wins. A test reads the key a slot publish carried with tb.out::<Slot>().with_options(..). Publishing and replies keys each pick list by its warehouse.

ack acknowledges a Pulsar delivery, retry negatively acknowledges it, and drop acknowledges it too: Pulsar has no terminal reject. The handler's outcome settles each delivery on its subscription. An acknowledged message moves the subscription's cursor past it, and the subscription does not deliver it again. A negative acknowledgement hands the message back to the subscription, not to the consumer that gave up on it: on a Shared subscription another consumer may take it. A message that should leave the subscription for good goes through a dead-letter policy, which drop does not need. The client queues acknowledgements and sends them in the background, so a settlement that returns is queued on the consumer, not yet confirmed by the broker. A message nobody settles comes back after the subscription's ack_timeout. retry_after asks for the delivery back after a delay. Acknowledgement settles the stock reservations of an inventory service by the handler's outcome.

Macros Manual examples/pulsar_settlement_ack.rs /// Reserves the stock of each order. `ack` acknowledges the message; `retry` negatively /// acknowledges it and the subscription delivers it again; `drop` acknowledges it as well, so an /// order of nothing is never seen again. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "fulfilment"))] async fn fulfil(order: &Order, State(warehouse): State<Warehouse>) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.quantity == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an order of nothing is dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } match warehouse.reserve(order).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "reservation failed, redelivering"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/pulsar_settlement_ack.rs /// Reserves the stock of each order. `Ok` acknowledges the message; `Err(retry)` negatively /// acknowledges it and the subscription delivers it again; `Err(drop)` acknowledges it as well, /// so an order of nothing is never seen again. struct Fulfil; impl Handle<Order, (), (), (), AppState> for Fulfil { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if order.quantity == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an order of nothing is dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } ctx.state().warehouse.reserve(order).await.map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "reservation failed, redelivering"); HandlerOutcome::retry() }) } }

ack_timeout redelivers a message left unacknowledged longer than the timeout; it also bounds the delay a retry_after may ask for. It is a setting of the PulsarSubscription descriptor and has no default: without it, an unsettled message comes back only when its consumer disconnects. With it, the client asks the broker for every message its handler has held longer than the timeout, whatever the reason: a handler that hangs, or a service that stopped mid-delivery. Each such redelivery counts toward the dead-letter cap, as a retry does. A retry_after delay that is not shorter than the timeout is refused when the handler returns it, with an error naming both values, because the timeout would bring the message back first. A handler keeps its backoff below the timeout for that reason. The in-process transport of a TestApp test applies the bound on retry_after; the redelivery itself happens on a broker. Acknowledgement bounds an unsettled delivery of an inventory service with an acknowledgement timeout.

An export the archive refused waits thirty seconds, inside the one-minute ack timeout of its subscription. max_attempts with dead_letter becomes the consumer's own dead-letter policy: the client moves a spent message, and the service publishes nothing. max_attempts(n) is how many times one message reaches the handler, the first delivery included. dead_letter(topic) is where it goes once those are spent. The Pulsar client counts the redeliveries, produces the spent message to that topic and acknowledges the original. A retry, a retry_after and an expired ack_timeout each advance the count. The two steps go together: a registration that writes one without the other refuses to start, and the error names the missing step. The broker counts redeliveries only where consumers compete for messages, so the cap belongs to a Shared or a KeyShared subscription. A registration that declares a cap over Exclusive or Failover refuses to start, and the error names the type. A handler mounted by a bare topic name declares the same pair, and one policy covers every topic of a multi-topic subscription. The client keeps the count to itself, so a handler cannot read how many deliveries a message has had. Retries and dead letters caps the deliveries of a refunds service and reads its dead letters.

retry_after(delay) holds the delivery unacknowledged in the service for the delay, then negatively acknowledges it; nothing is republished. A Pulsar negative acknowledgement carries no delay of its own, so the wait happens in the service. When it is over, the subscription delivers the same message again, with its own payload, properties and position. The redelivery is an ordinary one, so a dead-letter policy counts it like any other. The wait runs on the runtime the broker connected on. A process that exits during the wait loses the wait, not the message: the broker delivers it again once the ack_timeout elapses, or at once when the consumer disconnects. A delay that is not shorter than the subscription's ack_timeout is refused when the handler returns it; a subscription with no ack_timeout accepts any delay. A test waits the delay out with tb.advance, in process on a paused clock and against a live broker in real time. Retries and dead letters holds a refund back while the card processor's rate limit is used up.

An invoice whose customer is missing waits in the service for the lag, /// then the broker delivers it again. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("invoices", "billing"))] async fn issue(invoice: &Invoice, State(directory): State<Directory>) -> HandlerOutcome { match directory.find(invoice.customer).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(invoice.id, %err, "customer not found, trying again later"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(REPLICATION_LAG) } } } examples/manual/pulsar_settlement_retry_after.rs /// How long a customer the directory has not replicated yet gets before the next try. const REPLICATION_LAG: Duration = Duration::from_secs(2); /// Issues each invoice. A topic in #[subscriber] joins the broker's default subscription on it; a PulsarSubscription carries every other setting. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the topic orders, which is persistent://public/default/orders. Pulsar reads a topic only through a named subscription, and a bare name names none, so the name comes from PulsarBroker::default_subscription. A bare name on a broker with no default subscription stops the service at startup with an error that names the setting. The subscription is a durable cursor on the server, and it is Shared: every handler and every instance of a service that joins it competes for its messages. Name it after the service that owns the cursor, because another service that names the same subscription shares its backlog. Every other setting of a subscription belongs to a descriptor, which goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument: Descriptor Reads PulsarSubscription::new one topic PulsarSubscription::topics a fixed list of topics PulsarSubscription::pattern every topic whose name matches a regular expression The manual form passes the name or the descriptor to subscriber(source, body). A subscription the service creates starts at the tip of its topics, and one that already exists resumes at its cursor; start_at moves it. The Pulsar client moves a delivery whose retries are spent to a dead-letter topic itself, so a registration on any of these forms declares its retries and publishes nothing. Topics and subscriptions builds a fulfilment service on one topic, a fixed list, a pattern and the short form.

The topic orders, read under the subscription orders-svc. A slice handler takes a batch the service assembles: full at the mount site's size, or closed batch_wait after its first delivery. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. The Pulsar client hands over one delivery at a time, so the batch is assembled in the service. A batch closes when it holds n deliveries, or when batch_wait has passed since its first delivery, whichever comes first. batch_wait is a setting of the descriptor, 10 ms by default; a longer wait gives fuller batches on a quiet topic, at the cost of latency. An idle subscription waits for the first delivery as long as it takes, so a batch is never empty. One outcome settles every delivery of the batch. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles delivery i with outcome i. workers(n) keeps up to n batches in flight at once. A batch body reads a PulsarBatchContext, which carries the seek handle and no per-delivery field. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles delivery by delivery. Acknowledgement records the stock counts of warehouse scans in batches.

PulsarSubscription::pattern reads every topic whose full name matches a regular expression, topics created later included. The expression is matched against the full name of each topic, so it is written in full: persistent://public/default/orders-.*. The client lists one namespace for it, the one the prefix names: persistent://acme/orders/.* reads acme/orders, and a pattern with no tenant/namespace/ part reads public/default. The client lists the topics again every 30 seconds and joins the subscription to each new match. A topic created after startup is read from the listing that finds it on, and what reached it before that listing is not delivered. A pattern has no single topic to name the subscription by, so it reports under the subscription's own name. The expression is checked at startup, and one that is not a valid regular expression, or whose tenant or namespace is itself a regular expression, stops the service before any call to the server. The settings and their defaults are those of PulsarSubscription, and a seek moves the cursor on every topic the pattern reads. Topics and subscriptions audits every regional order topic, those created later included.

Every orders-* topic is recorded byte for byte, whatever its producer wrote; returns is not.
